1.title: TI Help
1.overview: Integrated technical support system (mobile, web, and desktop) built as a capstone project, replacing decentralized WhatsApp/email support with a single flow for opening and tracking tickets, with AI-assisted triage.
1.challenge: IT support was scattered across channels with no traceability or status visibility — users resent the same request through different channels when they got no response, and technicians received tickets with no standardized context.
1.process: In-person discovery with 11 sponsor users (7 Systems Analysis students, 2 from another cohort, 2 from Psychology). In the first version of the flow, users picked their own ticket priority (low/medium/high) — in discussion with professors and the 4-person team, we spotted a structural bias before even testing: users would tend to always mark 'high priority' to get served faster, invalidating triage. We fixed it by removing self-assigned priority, replacing it with problem type selection (hardware/software/network) + free description, leaving priority to triage (AI + technician). This was the only one of the 4 deliverables run with a formal backlog over the 6-month project.

designSprint.description: Pain-point gathering with professors and the 4-person team, mapping failures in the WhatsApp/email support flow before any wireframe existed.
Consolidated 11 interviews into problem definitions and identified the priority self-assignment bias before the first prototype.
Information architecture, triage flows, and high-fidelity prototypes in Figma across all three platforms (mobile, web, desktop).
Moderated in-person test with the 11 sponsor users and faculty panel, measuring task time before and after the menu repositioning.
Final delivery as a capstone project scoring 8.5/10, including a real mobile implementation in React Native.

1.myRole: UX/UI Designer and mobile front-end developer on a 4-person team, responsible for user research, information architecture, flows, high-fidelity prototypes, and the mobile implementation in React Native.

certainties: Users didn't know the status of an already-open ticket, causing repeated resubmission across channels
Letting users self-assign priority would create systematic bias toward 'high priority'
Technicians needed clear categorization (hardware/software/network) for fast triage
suppositions: AI-assisted categorization would reduce manual triage time
Repositioning notifications and the menu would reduce task execution time in the app
doubts: Would the triage AI stay accurate at real volume, outside the controlled test environment?
Would non-technical users (e.g. Psychology students) adapt to the flow as well as Systems Analysis students in the long run?

1.userFlow: User identifies the problem → selects type (hardware/software/network) and describes it → ticket gets categorized and prioritized by triage → user tracks status in real time. Technician flow (Web/Desktop): if there's no time to open the ticket immediately, it automatically enters as low-priority/waiting, configurable manually or with a later AI suggestion. Admin panel: employee creation, deletion, and updates restricted to admin, including deleting data of former employees — the biggest governance win the team identified.

personas.name: Systems Analysis participant
personas.pain: Opened tickets via WhatsApp and email without knowing if anyone was handling the issue, resending the same message across channels.
personas.goal: Open and track a ticket on any device, with visible status, without having to chase anyone.

personas.name: Psychology participant
personas.pain: Struggled to describe technical problems using specific vocabulary, which delayed service.
personas.goal: Report a problem in plain language, without needing to know IT terminology.

userStories.story: As a technical system user, I want to track my ticket's status in real time so that I don't have to resend the same request across different channels.
As a non-technical user, I want to describe my problem in my own words so that I don't need IT terminology to get help.

problemDefinitions.definition: Is a technical system user who needs real-time status visibility because it removes the need to manually chase support across multiple channels.
Is an IT-unfamiliar user who needs a plain-language ticket flow because technical jargon discourages them from asking for help early.

craftNotes.conventions: Followed navigation patterns users already internalize (bottom tab bar, bell icon for notifications, numeric badge for pending items) to reduce the learning curve for a mixed audience of technical and non-technical users.
craftNotes.affordances: Ticket-opening buttons use elevation and accent color to signal clickability; ticket status is communicated through color + icon + text simultaneously, never color alone, avoiding ambiguity for users who don't map color to state instantly.
craftNotes.equity: The flow was designed with non-technical users (Psychology students) in mind from the first version — removing self-assigned priority came directly from not wanting to penalize people who don't know how to 'game' the support system.
craftNotes.testing: The team reported in-person task observation and an informal time comparison before and after repositioning the menu and notifications. Timing was not instrumented per session.

1.solution: Removed user self-assigned priority → replaced with problem type selection + free description. Repositioned notifications and menu in the mobile version. Technician flow with an automatic waiting/low-priority state for tickets without immediate attention. Employee management and data deletion restricted to admin.
1.finalProject: BEFORE vs. AFTER METRIC (in-person test, 11 participants + faculty panel): time to complete the app's main tasks dropped from just over 5 minutes to 3 minutes 30 seconds — a ~30% reduction — after repositioning the menu/notifications. SUCCESS RATE: 100% maintained in both versions (before and after) — meaning the gain was in EFFICIENCY, not COMPLETION; nobody failed to complete the task before the change, it just took longer. ERROR IDENTIFIED AND FIXED: priority self-assignment bias, resolved during Reflect before formal testing even happened. ACADEMIC EVALUATION: 8.5/10 from the capstone panel. STATED LIMITATION: timing was measured informally, without per-session instrumented stopwatch tracking — directional data reported by the team and panel, not an instrumented usability test with per-task timing.

Identify what information would help users and technicians during triage.
Assess the clarity of the ticket creation and tracking flow.

People with less technical familiarity needed to describe issues in plain language.

Individual interview durations and transcripts are not documented; no verbatim quotations are available.

howMightWe: How might we centralize ticket creation and tracking without requiring people to know IT terminology?
How might we support triage without allowing self-assigned priority to distort it?

methods: Flow review with faculty and the project team based on the identified support problems.
ideas: Replace user-selected priority with an issue type and free-text description, leaving prioritization to triage.

Let non-technical users describe the issue in their own words.

Technician: ticket queue → triage → support → update status.

findings: The team reported that main tasks went from just over 5 minutes to about 3 minutes 30 seconds after repositioning the menu and notifications; this is directional, informal timing.
Completion was reported as 100% before and after; the reported gain was time, not task completion.

iterations.problem: The choice could be biased toward high priority.

iterations.after: Triage assigns priority using the information provided.

iterations.before: The menu and notifications were placed less efficiently for the observed tasks.
iterations.problem: The team reported longer completion times for the main tasks.
iterations.decision: Reposition the menu and notifications in the mobile version.
iterations.after: The informal comparison reported less task time; the timing was not instrumented.

results.label: A mobile version was implemented in React Native as part of the capstone project.
Reported task time: just over 5 min before and about 3 min 30 sec after repositioning; timing was informal.

learnings: Status visibility is part of the support service, not just an interface detail.
Triage should reduce bias while allowing people without technical vocabulary to describe problems.
nextSteps: Instrument task-based evaluation and document the script, timing, and sample.
Evaluate AI-assisted triage accuracy across different scenarios and volumes.
limitations: Academic project in a bounded setting; results do not demonstrate production performance.
Reported task times are directional and were not instrumented per session.

2.title: KaloBurn
2.overview: A conceptual mobile fitness product connecting practitioners with training, professionals, plans, and progress tracking. This case combines the existing interface with one documented exploratory interview; opportunities are hypotheses, not population-level research findings.
2.challenge: The interviewed participant plans A/B/C workouts in advance but adapts each session when experiencing fatigue or pain, finding equipment unavailable, or running short on time. The design challenge is to support that flexibility while preserving progress tracking through loads and repetitions.
2.process: One exploratory interview was conducted with an experienced gym/CrossFit practitioner. The account was synthesized into behaviors, pain points, and opportunities, then related to the mobile structure shown in the board: workout flow, professional discovery, and progress tracking. This is qualitative evidence from one person, not broad product validation.

designSprint.description: Exploratory interview with one experienced practitioner; A/B/C planning, in-session adaptations, and personal progress measures.
Separated evidence reported by one person from hypotheses that need testing with other profiles.
Opportunity: keep a workout useful when equipment, physical condition, or time requires an adjustment.
Connected discovery, professionals, plans, active workout, schedule, messages, and progress as represented in the interface.
Explored a mobile experience for viewing workouts, recording activity, and tracking progress.
Conceptual. The flow still needs to be tested with practitioners; no formal test is documented.

2.myRole: UX/UI Designer; exploratory interview, synthesis, and case structure.

certainties: In the exploratory interview, the participant reported planning A/B/C workouts roughly every two months and adapting sessions to the day's context.
The participant mainly tracks progress through load and repetitions.
Unavailable equipment can lead the participant to switch exercises or skip part of the workout.
suppositions: Alternatives related to available equipment may help keep a session moving.
Linking load and repetitions to workout history may make progression easier to interpret.
Optional points and challenges may support motivation for people interested in healthy competition.
doubts: How can exercises be adapted safely without recommending changes that conflict with physical limitations?
Which indicators are useful to practitioners with different routines and goals?
Would gamification motivate without pressuring people who prefer to train without competition?

2.userFlow: Plan A/B/C workout → arrive at the gym → check equipment → adapt or follow the exercise → record load and repetitions → compare with previous sessions → adjust the next workout.

personas.name: Experienced, adaptive practitioner
personas.role: Behavioral archetype derived from the single documented exploratory interview; not representative of a population.
personas.pain: Needs to reorganize a 1–1.5-hour session when the gym is busy, equipment is unavailable, or their body calls for an adjustment.
personas.goal: Keep a flexible plan and understand progress through load and repetitions without relying on a rigid routine.

userStories.story: As a practitioner, I want to see an alternative when planned equipment is unavailable so I can adapt the session without losing workout context.
As a practitioner, I want to compare load and repetitions across sessions so I can decide when progression may make sense.

problemDefinitions.definition: Needs to adjust a plan when facing fatigue, pain, unavailable equipment, or limited time because completing the session exactly as planned is not always possible.

craftNotes.conventions: The provided board shows mobile navigation for home, explore, workouts, messages, and profile, plus detail and progress screens.
craftNotes.affordances: In the exploration, exercise alternatives and their rationale should appear alongside unavailable equipment; this is an interface hypothesis to validate.
craftNotes.equity: Adaptations must respect pain and perceived limitations, and avoid presenting an automated suggestion as medical advice or professional prescription.
craftNotes.testing: One exploratory interview is documented. No formal usability test was conducted or documented.

2.solution: The design direction preserves the areas for discovery, professionals, workouts, schedule, messages, and progress represented in the board. As a future opportunity, it proposes linking the planned workout to alternatives when equipment is busy, and recording load and repetitions for comparison. These adaptations are hypotheses, not validated features.
2.finalProject: Conceptual design outcome informed by one exploratory interview. No formal usability test or impact metrics are documented. The board shows a mobile experience for discovery, workouts, schedule, messages, and progress.
2.conclusion: One person's account suggests that a workout plan needs room for adaptation: equipment availability, fatigue, pain, and time all influence a session. The interface can support decisions while keeping the practitioner in control. Broadening the research and testing the adaptation flow are next steps, not completed outcomes.

objectives: Understand how the participant plans and adapts workouts.

problemStatement.because: Occupied equipment, fatigue, pain, and a limited workout window can make the original plan impractical.

howMightWe: How might we help a practitioner adapt a workout when equipment is unavailable?

How might we combine guidance and flexibility without making workouts rigid?
How might points and challenges support healthy competition without pressuring people who do not want to compete?

3.title: DN Jeans
3.overview: DN Jeans is a product-discovery experience designed to help customers browse catalog items, compare options and move more easily toward purchase without unnecessary friction.
3.challenge: The challenge is to guide discovery through categories, filters, and product details toward a clear decision while respecting the brand's documented direct WhatsApp conversion context.
3.process: Retrospective UX reconstruction based on the available product material and screen boards. No formal interviews or usability tests are documented. The proposed journey organizes discovery, comparison, and decision-making without presenting design hypotheses as customer research.

designSprint.description: Retrospective review of the catalog, available screens, and the WhatsApp conversion behavior recorded in the project.
Design hypothesis: reduce the effort between finding an item and gathering enough information to decide.
Proposed organization across home, category/listing, product detail, and purchase decision.
Provided boards show desktop and mobile explorations, including cart and checkout.
No formal test is documented. The choice between checkout and direct contact needs confirmation with the brand.

3.myRole: UX reconstruction, content structure, and visual product design.

certainties: The available material includes home, category/listing, product detail, and cart/checkout explorations.
The project records direct WhatsApp contact as a brand conversion behavior.
No formal user research or usability testing is documented.
suppositions: Visible filters and attributes may make product comparison easier.
Size, color, and availability details may reduce questions before contact.
A WhatsApp CTA may better match the recorded direct-conversion behavior than requiring checkout.
doubts: The brand's preference for WhatsApp contact needs confirmation given the cart and checkout screens in the boards.
There is no documented evidence about which filters or information customers prioritize.

3.userFlow: Home → category/listing → filter and compare → product detail → decide → contact/convert. Cart and checkout appear in boards as explorations and are not presented as a validated flow.

personas.name: Catalog explorer
personas.role: Conceptual persona / design hypothesis; not derived from documented interviews.
personas.pain: May need to move between listings, product details, and contact to clarify information.
personas.goal: Find an item, check relevant attributes, and choose how to proceed.

userStories.story: As a visitor, I want to filter and compare items so I can find options that match what I am looking for.

problemDefinitions.definition: A catalog visitor may need categories, attributes, and a clear next step to move from discovery to a decision.

craftNotes.conventions: The visual foundation stays consistent with a familiar e-commerce rhythm: product categories, imagery, pricing and decision-oriented product details.
craftNotes.affordances: Filters, product attributes and action CTAs stay visible and easy to evaluate to reduce hesitation mid-browse.
craftNotes.equity: The flow respects the brand's real conversion behavior by keeping the close-out step in WhatsApp rather than forcing a cart-based checkout model.
craftNotes.testing: No formal usability testing data exists for the original project, so this is framed as a proposed UX improvement rather than a claimed validated outcome.

3.solution: The proposal organizes discovery across home, categories/listing, comparison, and product details. Direct WhatsApp contact remains the conversion path recorded in the project; cart and checkout are presented as alternatives explored in the boards, not as a validated decision.
3.finalProject: Product-design case with a UX reconstruction and desktop/mobile boards. No customer research or formal test is documented; no conversion outcomes are attributed to the design.
3.conclusion: Discovery → category → comparison → detail → decision. The flow and boards provide a basis for structuring the catalog. The relationship between checkout and WhatsApp support needs alignment with the brand's commercial process and validation before being treated as a final solution.

7.solution: The work brought together editorial strategy, creative production, and content management for a client's political Instagram profile. The client testimonial reports 10K views on one post and 47.7K reach in the most recent quarter, roughly 29% above the previous quarter; independent data is not available to attribute this change to a specific intervention.
7.finalProject: Real content and design project for a client's Instagram profile. According to the client's testimonial, one post reached 10K views and the most recent quarter reached 47.7K, roughly 29% above the previous period. Exact dates and supporting analytics are not available in this case.
